summary:
Albania does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or gender expression. Homosexuality carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995, and the 2010 anti-discrimination law extended protection on the ground of sexual orientation; that law did not introduce same-sex marriage, which remains unavailable. There is no sourced record of criminal exposure for visitors on grounds of gender identity or expression, and no sourced record of police targeting of trans people.

International review of Albania's sexual-orientation and gender-identity record is unusually open. The UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, conducted a country visit from 1 to 12 July 2024 and issued an end-of-mission statement assessing good practices and challenges with recommendations to the State; his full report, A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 of 17 June 2025, evaluates Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards using information gathered before, during and after the visit.

The documented violence picture is specific and adverse for trans people. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 records that the organisation Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people during the review period. In the same period, discrimination complaints filed over screenings of the film 'Strange World' were mediated, with the Anti-Discrimination Commissioner ruling in favour in one case, and community groups ran support schemes including food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV.

The realistic visitor risk is social hostility rather than legal exposure. No bathroom or facilities restriction is sourced, no entry or visa rule keyed to gender marker is sourced, and no screening practice that would out a trans traveller at the border is documented. Political hostility toward LGBT visibility does appear in the public record: in July 2021 Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a 'suspicious, revolting agenda', and MP Nard Ndoka posted that the government was 'LGBT' and was pushing LGBT values in schools. Earlier, in October 2011, the Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded Democratic Party MP Tritan Shehu for telling parliament that 'homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones', warning him to avoid remarks creating an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community. An annual Pride is held in Tirana.
tangentialFactors:
The trajectory of Albanian law is one of removal rather than expansion of penalty: the ten-year sentence for homosexuality was abolished in 1995, and the anti-discrimination statute arrived in 2010 without marriage equality attached. Prime Minister Sali Berisha had voiced support for same-sex marriage in July 2009, framing the measure as EU-integration driven, which situates reform pressure in Albania's candidacy process rather than in domestic litigation.

Political rhetoric is the sharpest turbulence factor. The 2021 schools-campaign row and the 2011 parliamentary slur both came from senior figures in the then-ruling or main opposition party, and in the 2011 instance the response came from the Anti-Discrimination Commissioner rather than from criminal process. Anti-LGBT messaging therefore operates as a reputational and electoral instrument, with the institutional counterweight being a mediation and reprimand mechanism.

Compared with regional peers, the July 2024 visit by the UN Independent Expert and the June 2025 follow-up report indicate a government willing to submit to international scrutiny, while ILGA-Europe's reporting indicates that implementation of the National LGBTI Action Plan (2021–2027) remains weak. EU candidate status is the standing external driver of alignment.
localsOnly:
Discrimination complaints are handled through the Anti-Discrimination Commissioner, whose mediation practice produced at least one favourable ruling in 2023 over complaints about screenings of the film 'Strange World'. The Commissioner has also used reprimand powers against a sitting MP for remarks framed as creating an atmosphere of tension toward LGBT people.

Community provision fills gaps in state care. Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people during the 2023 review year, and support schemes operated by civil-society groups included distribution of food packages to trans sex workers and to people living with HIV.

The National LGBTI Action Plan 2021–2027 is the governing policy framework, with documented shortcomings in implementation. High-school LGBT education work has been the target of coordinated parliamentary attacks from the opposition, including claims that such groups carry a 'suspicious, revolting agenda'. An annual Pride takes place in Tirana.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether Albanian anti-discrimination law names gender identity as a protected ground alongside sexual orientation, or whether protection for trans visitors rests on other provisions. This is unsourced here rather than absent.

No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, change of name or gender marker on passports and identity documents, entry or visa screening keyed to gender marker, or facilities and bathroom rules for trans people. Nothing should be inferred from silence on any of these points.

The count of ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people comes from ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 covering 2023 and reflects cases logged by one organisation; the inventory does not establish national incidence, police recording practice, or outcomes in those cases. Similarly, the claim that no documented police targeting exists rests on the absence of such reporting in the reviewed material, not on a dedicated audit.

The end-of-mission statement of 12 July 2024 and report A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 of 17 June 2025 are described from their titles and scope statements; their specific findings and recommendations were not read for this record.
